Phainon politely declined the crew's offers of refreshments and the lounge, choosing to head out. He had an errand to run.

Even the most popular people in the city needed to go grocery shopping for their hot grumpy roommates. Phainon didn't make the rules. Mydei did. The shelves were laden with condiments Phainon usually never bought because he just didn't have the time or energy. Posters titled "Okhema's hope" were plastered on the window of the store. Phainon felt a wave of embarrassment when he first laid eyes on one of those posters.

People had always noticed him— at least, half the city did. But this was different. Everyone's eyes were now on him.

"Carrots… check. Onions— now where did they put the onions?"

Phainon bent over the crates, trying to locate the onions. At tap on his shoulder made him jolt.

He pulled his mask back up and spun around to face some of his classmates. Not the press or the general public. Good. He's had to be extremely careful recently to avoid being swarmed.

A blonde haired girl spoke up."Do you want to go to the party we're hosting tonight?"

"I— " He paused.

Phainon had to get back to Mydei.

"No, I'm sorry. I can't do that today. Have fun!"

Normally, he would have agreed to spare the person's feelings. But why should he? He had important things to get home to.

✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ 𖥔 ݁☀️𖥔 ݁✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆

Four days later

Miss Tribios had informed them earlier that day that they were partnered up for yet another mission— this time, to no resistance.

Mydei took off his helmet and removed his leather jacket. Phainon turned around and squinted up at the wall, the glare of the sun burning his eyes. He would rather burn his eyes and bleach his brain than ogle at Mydei's muscular arms.

"What're you trying to do, staring up at the sun like that?" Mydei questioned "Burning my eyes." Phainon responded simply.

"…"

"…"

"Why?"

Without even looking at him,Phainon could tell Mydei was beyond perplexed. He was probably cocking his head to the side and trying to understand Phainon's actions. Phainon's heart squeezed a little at that mental image.

"No reason." Phainon chirped in a voice too upbeat and high to be his own.

He then scaled the wall and stood at the top, grinning down at Mydei. "What do you think, Mydei? I practised."

Mydei seemed lost in thought, gazing at Phainon with an indescribable look on his face. He climbed up the wall too, his hair fluttering in the wind.

"Not bad." Mydei said after they descended onto the soft grass.

Phainon scanned the area for Black Tide creatures. The breeze was rather strong that day and grey clouds were already sweeping in. He could hear soft rustling but he couldn't find the source of that sound. He nearly jumped out of his skin when Mydei's hand tapped his shoulder.

"There are two groups— there." Mydei pointed to the right "And there" Mydei pointed straight ahead at the dense foliage.

Phainon sputtered, still calming his rapidly beating heart— the reason definitely not being Mydei's proximity, "How did you—"

"I didn't train for wars by playing board games and chatting over coffee, HKS"

"Alright, I'll go straight ahead and you go right. Shout my name if you need help."

Mydei quirked an eyebrow "I don't recall you being the team leader. As far as I'm concerned, I was the one who pointed out the creatures." He held up both hands, as if in resignation "But fine, I'll do as you say, just this once. Try not to get yourself killed out there, Deliverer."

"You too."

Phainon took a deep breath before heading in the direction Mydei pointed out. A shrill screech cut through the air.

Phainon points Dawnmaker in the direction of the sound. A Black Tide creature lunged at him. He deflected the hit and stabbed it in the chest. Letting one last guttural screech, it fell silent.

It was like the rest of the forest came alive, Black Tide creatures swarming him in hordes. Phainon hacked his way through them with ease. It's strange, he thought to himself as he sidestepped a rolling severed limb, how the number of creatures have grown exponentially.

The Black Tide had stopped its erosion by now, so where did so many Black Tide monsters even come from?

He did a quick headcount of the creatures he'd killed— fifty five. Phainon was pretty sure he finished his job.

A laboured gasp came from behind a tree. Phainon approached it cautiously, Dawnmaker at the ready. A woman lay on the floor, coughing weakly. Phainon paled— citizens of Okhema don't ever wander outside the walls. So this woman must be a refugee. Her eyes darted up at Phainon and swiveled about frantically, like a cornered animal.

"Hello? I'm going to be bringing you back to Okhema, okay?" Phainon attempted to pacify her, placing Dawnmaker on the grass and holding both of his arms up to show that he meant no harm.

Her ragged breathing didn't cease. In fact, it didn't look like she understood what Phainon said.

Phainon fired off a quick email to Mydei.

Phainon ˂phainon.419@email.com˃10:57AM to Mydei▼

Go to the facility and arrange medical help for a person in the outskirts. Go without me, I'll get back on my own with her.

Phainon kneeled to the ground, his heart twisting painfully when the woman flinched. She reminded him too much of himself when he was younger. He had promised to never let anyone have to suffer the way he did — so he became someone who promised hope and safety.

But it felt like he failed her.

What was the point of trying to protect everyone if he failed to protect a single person?

Phainon didn't know how long it took, but he eventually coaxed her into trusting him enough to let him escort her to safety. As the woman stood up shakily, Phainon spotted a small building in the distance. Must be one of the watch towers stationed around the perimeter. The woman stumbled and Phainon rushed to help her.

"What's your name?" Phainon prodded gently, offering her a bottle of water.

The woman said nothing, guzzling down the water like it was the first and last time she's ever had water.

It wasn't much, but it was a start.

She gawked at the sight of the facility when they finally approached it. He led her into the med bay, braving his way past the curious stares. Hyacine wasn't on shift, but the other nurses instantly snapped up to help the woman.

After ensuring her safety, Phainon headed off in search of Mydei. He poked his head into possible rooms where Mydei could be. When his search started feeling fruitless, Phainon considered the possibility of Mydei getting back to the apartment. He aimlessly wandered through the garage before he heard a familiar voice.

"I'm right behind you"

There he was, in all his radiant glory— hair like spun gold, its ends dipped crimson. Phainon's face broke into a huge grin.

"So, how many did you kill?" He asked, practically skipping over to Mydei. If he seemed desperate, so be it.

"So we're not addressing the email you sent me?"

"Oh, right, there was this woman beyond Okhema's borders. She's probably a refugee or got lost. I decided to bring her back with me and arrange a medical examination. If she's all clear, she can live in the refugee camp until she can get back on her feet."

"As expected of the Deliverer."

There was no bite to Mydei's words, rather, a warmth that made Phainon's head spin.

"Ah, I'll go check in on the lady— the preliminary medical test results should be out soon. See you in the apartment?" Phainon asked.

"Yes, see you." Mydei hopped on his bike and drove away.

Phainon was heading up the stairs when a shrill screech cut through the air. Screams followed— the sound making Phainon's blood run cold. Red flooded his peripheral vision as alarms blared. Fear coiled in his gut as he sprinted towards the source of the sound. His mind raced through the possibility of what could've happened. His footfalls felt slowed, weighed down by apprehension. His lungs couldn't take in enough oxygen to sustain his panic. Others in the facility ran the other way, trying to flee the building as fast as they could. Phainon just ran towards the destruction.

And if the fire killed him, then so be it.

He felt sick to his very being when he heard yet another scream erupt from the closed door of the med bay. Slamming himself against the door, he staggered into the room and froze when he saw the pool of red gather at his feet.

Blood.

There was so much blood.

Blood splattered the pristine white shelves of the med bay, cascaded down the walls and pooled onto the ground. The room was bathed in crimson.

Tears pricked his eyes when he registered the desecrated corpses littering the room. A body was flung at him and weakly thumped against the wall before falling to the ground like a swallow shot out of the sky. Ribs protruded from the nurse's body as he made a gurgling sound, blood and froth escaping his mouth before his eyes rolled up and turned glassy.

A Black Tide creature stood at the center of it, ripping off someone's arm and gnawing the bone. Sickening crunches filled the room as it shattered the bone and chewed it. Its eyes roved around the room before focusing on Phainon. Those eyes had the same disoriented, terrified quality the woman he'd escorted had.

Oh.

Oh.

The monster advanced on him and all he could do in that moment was remain frozen in his spot. He was catatonic as it neared him.

This was it. This was the end.

Finally, his survival instincts— honed after years of surviving in Styxia— finally kicked in.

He moved out of the way as it attacked and cut it down with Dawnmaker.

The monster that paraded as human breathed its last, just like its victims had. It was just him, standing in the middle of a scene he never wanted to be a part of again. He did exactly what he did when he was younger, standing in a room with his family's dead bodies. He left.

Like the coward he was.

Phainon felt like he was in a grainy slow motion horror film as he watched the ambulances pull up to the building.Something curled in his insides, making him want to rip them out— tear his lungs open and let the pain flow freely. Throat constricting so hard he thought he might choke, the grief swelled in his body like a surging tide with no way out. That tide burnt him from the inside, it existed in every breath.

He didn't register much, just the bodies being carried out and the panic that followed. Wrapped in white, the flesh and bone encasing of what used to be their consciousness was all that was left of the victims; their life's story reduced to the way they died.

He could only hope that death was kind.

Phainon felt too numb to cry at the funeral.

The drones that reported the incident flew above the attendees. Huge screens placed all over the city reported the incident for all to see.

"Incident.. at the CHRYSOS institute… three found dead… suspected Black Tide monster attack.." The screens blared.

"Okhema is no longer safe! Look! Even the safest institute— our protectors — got attacked, so what about us?" A reporter cried out

He stood among the sea of mourners, the crowd suffocating like a thick blanket on a hot summer's day. The families of the deceased stood at the forefront, sobbing uncontrollably over their graves. The grief of their families must be unfathomable, a pain beyond what Phainon felt.

A sound similar to the siren blared before all the screens in Okhema were taken over by an emergency broadcast. The Council of Elders' emergency report, the screens displayed before a spokesperson sat before a table, adjusting the her glasses.

"We have received intel about the tragedy at CHRYSOS institute. Video footage of a certain recruit has surfaced, where he leads a Black Tide creature in disguise into the facility."

Phainon saw his face on the big screen, where he guided the woman into the facility. It cut to a video of him rushing further into the building as everyone else ran out. Finally, a grainy picture of him leaving the scene, covered in blood.

"If this is the person you entrust your lives and futures to, I implore you to reconsider. First, he led three people to their deaths. Second, he didn't take accountability for the incident. Your so called Deliverer has failed you. Tell me again, what is the CHRYSOS institute supposed to stand for? Hope? Is this really hope? Is there even any use keeping it up and running?"

They knew.

Everyone knew.

Everything Phainon worked so hard to build— the reputation, the trust, the sense of safety— came tumbling down that very moment.

Eyes swiveled around to focus on him, their glares of contempt burned holes into his skin as he stood rooted in place. His heart felt like it could sink no more out of the sheer panic dragging it down. The next thing he registered was the crowd parting to give way to a woman with pure rage in her eyes. She grabbed the front of his shirt and shook him.

"YOU KILLED MY SON!" She screamed in a raw, broken voice

Phainon wanted to protest— he had enough strength to break free, but he felt too weak to try. She was right, he killed her son. The crowd shifted around him, craning their heads at the scene. Yet, they maintained a distance from him, creating what felt like a black hole of space around him. Nobody dared cross the invisible circle. He was something to watch, to gawk at and to hate.

"HOW COULD YOU TAKE HIM AWAY FROM US? HOW DARE YOU!" She cried, her hands snaking around his throat like a vine. Phainon let out a choked sound as her hands pressed down. He bit the inside of his mouth, trying to dampen his reaction. He didn't want anyone to think he was begging for pity if he looked wretched enough.

Crying would only garner more revulsion, for he was a vile thing beyond redemption.

"I'm sorry" Was all he could say.

"SORRY? Is that all you have to say to me?"

Phainon flinched, squeezing his eyes shut and preparing himself for the full force of her rage.

He slowly opened his eyes as he felt her jolt and retract her hands. She looked horrified at what she'd just done— staggering back. The crowd murmured and shifted, but he couldn't catch a word they were saying. He numbly lifted a hand to his throat. Someone was near his leg. Phainon glanced down.

A little boy looked up at him, eyes red rimmed and implored in a quiet voice, "Can you bring my sister back?"

Phainon's heart shattered. How could he not feel such a deep sense of connect to the little boy— Phainon himself was in his shoes once, clinging to every hope that his family would magically be alive. He cursed the Black Tide, swore that when he grew up, he'd avenge their deaths.

Phainon was just as bad as the Tide's monsters in the child's eyes.

"No." Phainon finally murmured.

"She's really gone, isn't she?" The kid asked in a wavering voice.

Phainon took a sharp breath, because yes, of course she was and he was to blame for it.

The boy's parents whisked him out of Phainon's line of sight, like Phainon was a radioactive substance that nobody wanted to get near to or touch. They glared at him— the message clear in their eyes— it should've been you, not her.

Phainon found himself agreeing wholeheartedly. It felt like he aged a million years in those few seconds. Some people talked to him, but their words flew over Phainon's head. He just wanted out. To where, he did not know, but he wanted to leave. The hum of people eventually surged to close in on him. Heavy footfalls approached him as Danae, one of his acquaintances, strode to him.

"What did you do, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?" Her voice sounded defeated; broken beyond repair. Wrath would've been easier for Phainon to sustain.

He took away her lover.

He truly was repulsive.

"What would you rather I say?" A voice that wasn't his, yet sounded unmistakeably his and coming from his own mouth, responded.

"Say that you regret it. Defend yourself— give me a reason to want you dead."

Phainon gave up.

What was all this for? First, his family. Next, all those lives he couldn't save in Styxia. Now this?

Trying was futile if all the outcomes led to the death of everyone but him.

"I suggest you leave." An icy voice broke through the crowd. It wasn't a suggestion, it was a command. The crowd parted to give way to a tall, imposing figure. Mydei had a feral look on his face. That was a look Phainon had never seen before. The people surrounding Phainon backed away. Mydei placed himself between Phainon and the families. The intent was clear— you have to get through me to get to him.

"Come on." He turned to Phainon, grabbing his hand and leading him away.

Once they were out of the crowd, Phainon wrenched his hand away and locked eyes with Mydei, a calm indifference settling over him.

"I don't need your help." He said coldly.

"Phainon— "

"Hate me all you want, just don't try to reason with me. Don't try to side with me or ask me for an explanation. Please."

"Please listen to what I have to say." Mydei argued, firm in his resolve.

Phainon took a few steps back, shaking his head. "No. This would be so much easier if you didn't pity me."

"But I don't pity you."

"Lies." Phainon smiled sweetly before he fled.

Phainon didn't want people to look at him in the pitying way they did when he was in Styxia. The wretched child, so young and afraid, they'd think. Phainon despised sympathy and as much as he felt like a horrible person for lashing out, he'd rather face anger than pity.

It was as he left the funeral that he realised that was the first time Mydei had called him by his name. Unnoticed, he went up to his old dorm room.

The room was almost fully repaired— the leaky pipe and sagging roof gone. Phainon remembered leaving behind some clothes and snacks that wouldn't fit into his suitcase. Yes, those would suffice. He could hide away from the rest of the world for as long as he wanted to.

In the mirror, he noticed red marks on his neck. His fingers brushed over them and rested on the sun tattoo. He had gotten that tattoo when he decided to commit to the role of Deliverer. Now, looking at the angry red marks that surrounded it, that dream felt more like naivety.

Phainon heard shouts from outside, so he pushed up the glass of his windows and looked down. There stood a mob of people, angrily shouting curses at him. They must've figured out where he went.

"Send him out! Let him live with the monsters!"

"Murderer!"

Security reached them, escorting them out. Their hatred lingered in the air long after they left. He could only imagine the disgust and regret Hyacine, Castorice, Aglaea, Tribios and Anaxa felt at having the misfortune of knowing him. Worst of all, Mydei— Kephale, he didn't even want to think about what Mydei wanted to tell him earlier.

Too numb to feel anything, he stared at the empty patch of grass.

He shut the window closed with a loud bang and let the tears he'd been holding back fall.

The skies wept along with him.

Rain pattered on the window, drowning out his sobs.

"I'm sorry" He told the empty room.

"I'm so sorry." He repeated to his revolting reflection in the mirror.

"Please forgive me." He said to no one at all, choking on his sobs.

Fifteen years ago

Cyrene drew up a card.

"The Chariot" She said. "It means determination and willpower" She smiled, baring her teeth, wild and carefree. Cyrene was happy, so he was too. He clapped and laughed with her.

"Phainon, some day you will be someone strong and powerful. You will fight for the sake of so many others." She ruffled his hair.

"Really?"

"Yep! Trust me, you'll do great!"

That naive child believed that he was capable of becoming something great.

✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ 𖥔 ݁☀️𖥔 ݁✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆

Six years ago

Sometimes, he liked to sneak into the remnants of a school in Styxia. He'd flip through the pages of the textbooks and read yellowed notes students used to pass to each other. Phainon would fantasise about continuing his schooling in Aedes Elysiae. He'd go to school in the mornings with Cyrene and run through the wheat fields to reach the only school in their tiny village. They'd sit under the big maple tree for some lessons or inside the building if it got too hot outside.

Phainon liked sitting outside better. It felt liberating to have the soft breeze tickle you.

Classes would be temporarily suspended in the harvesting seasons so the students could help their parents catch fish or harvest crops. Not many children lived there; more than half of them moved out to the big city when they became adults. There was only one teacher, Miss Pythias. She would let them out to play once school was done. That was the highlight of Phainon's day.

And then, reality would wash over him like a bucket of ice cold water.

Aedes Elysiae and everyone in it were long gone. Yes, Aedes Elysiae itself wasn't fully lost to the Black Tide because there wasn't much of it to be destroyed. But the people? The ones who made that place home?

They were dead— Phainon being the bearer of their memory, the only one left to tell their stories.

He would sneak back out of the school and chastise himself for being so out of it because now the rations for dinner are probably gone.

Phainon kicked a pebble down the streets of Styxia aimlessly. On his back was a sharp chunk of metal he'd broken off a crumbling structure— he used it to fight. He wore clothes he scavenged from bags that belonged to people who didn't live to see another sunrise. Morally questionable, yes, but morals? In this wasteland? Perish that thought.

He reached his makeshift home— the location changed every few weeks because stagnation killed. Bidding goodbye to his new pebble friend, he pushed up the window and climbed into the building. The door to the building and several other rooms were completely destroyed, but there were a few fully intact.

Structural integrity be damned.

He knelt onto the sheets of a makeshift bed and took off his bag. Inside it was the rations he'd secured for himself. Phainon broke off a piece of stale bread and opened a can of olives far beyond its expiration date. Not the most appetising meal, but it would do. Midway through his meal, a sharp rap hit the window.

His stomach lurched.

Stuffing the rest of his meal into his mouth, he scrambled to his feet. If that was a Black Tide monster, he was ready to face it. The knock sounded again. Black Tide creatures didn't have manners, so this must be a human. Most of the others in Styxia minded their own business and only swooped in to scavenge through the belongings of the deceased.

This person might be dangerous.

"Hello? Is anyone there?" A dignified voice that sounded like it belonged to a noble lady came from the other side.

"I can see your shadow, no point in hiding" A younger, cheekier female voice teased.

These people weren't from here. It wouldn't end well if he ignored them and Phainon knew how to escape and fight back. He would be fine.

"Uh— Yes. Hi." He responded, wincing at how coarse his voice sounded.

"See? I told you he went in here."

Had they been following him?

The noble lady cleared her throat. "Can we come in?"

Phainon couldn't talk to those people dressed the way he was. He didn't want them to think of him as some poor soul who lived a life of suffering— a project for them to take back home and show off like a trophy. Deciding that he needed to look more presentable, he pulled out a wrinkled button up shirt he found the other day.

"One minute" He called out, changing into the shirt. "Okay, yes, you can come in now."

He stepped back cautiously as a grey haired girl with a cat eared hoodie climbed in first. A golden haired woman with the strangest pair of green eyes he had ever seen followed her. The noble lady looked exactly what her voice sounded like— regal in every way and terribly out of place in this wasteland.

"My name is Aglaea." She introduced herself "Neat place you have there, little guy." The grey haired girl commented, whizzing through the room, prodding at wires and cobwebbed furniture.

"That's Cipher" Aglaea gestured to the girl, who busied herself with upturning her jacket and counting the little trinkets she'd collected.

Phainon shifted awkwardly "Hello, I'm Phainon. It's not really my place, I'm just here for a while."

"Do you live here with anyone else? Like a parent or a friend or a sibling?"

"No. It's just me."

"… I see. And how long have you been here for?"

Phainon counted the number of years he'd spent here on his fingers, holding up a finger for each year he remembered.

He held up three fingers."I'm guessing three."

"And you are currently?"

"Sixteen or seventeen."

"Hm."

Phainon felt his cheeks burn. Sure, he wasn't the healthiest teenager, but he was pretty tall— taller than most people around here. So surely, he looked old enough.

"Nice shirt." Cipher giggled from behind him.

Great. Now, what was wrong with his shirt?

Sensing his exasperation, she pointed to the back of the shirt and snorted "I'm sure you didn't want 'kick me' written on the back of it. Permanent marker, I think. Bold choice."

Mortification washed over him. He squeezed his eyes shut, trying to pretend like this encounter wasn't real and nothing ever happened. When he opened his eyes again and saw the same two people, he gave up on that fleeting hope.

"Why are you two even here? This isn't exactly a tourist destination. Most people want out." He asked, tugging at the fraying threads of the linen shirt.

"I've founded an institute— CHRYSOS. We aim to eliminate the Black Tide that plagues Amphoreus. Currently, we're bringing refugees from all over Amphoreus to Okhema for safety."

"And I happened to be the first guinea pig you laid eyes on?"

"Actually, you're the last."

"Huh?"

No wonder the streets felt so empty. There weren't many other people in Styxia to begin with, and the numbers kept dwindling as more and more people dropped dead. Phainon used to think that it was inevitable that he would be the last man standing.

Aglaea nodded and explained,"We heard about this white haired teenager who fought against Black Tide creatures and protected the people here. You're a truly selfless and noble person, Phainon"

Noble? Selfless? No, that was stretching it. He just didn't want people to die to the creatures, maybe give them one less thing to worry about. That was what his Ma taught him. He was just trying to be less of a bad son to her.

"You were a tricky one to find, I'll give you that" Cipher said, resuming her position at Aglaea's side.

"Uh, thanks?"

Phainon was getting distracted, so he dragged his mind back to his original train of thought "Wait, is this some elaborate recruitment scheme to get me into your program? If so, I refuse to be your toy."

"No. We're bringing you back to Okhema like everyone else in Styxia because safety is a human's basic right. If you choose to join our program, that decision would be yours to make." Aglaea said firmly.

"Oh. Um—" Phainon stared at the ground.

"What're you waiting for, little guy? Come on!" Cipher picked up Phainon's bag and tossed it to him.

Phainon fumbled with the bag before following them out.

As he took a seat in the train that led them to Okhema, Phainon realised that this was really happening. He was really getting out of Styxia. There was a weight that settled in his heart that pushed down the hope— just how much he owed Aglaea for saving him.

"I'll join your program." He said after much deliberation.

Aglaea was pleasantly surprised "That's great. You'll be enrolled once we reach Okhema." She offered him a small smile.

Perhaps this was a chance to prove himself invaluable, he mused, admiring the forests the train sped by. He could protect other people— properly, this time.

Nobody would have their futures stolen from them, not if he could help it.

Years later, that last ember of childish hope was snuffed out. Once reality truly set in and glamour wore off, a bone deep exhaustion settled.

✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ 𖥔 ݁☀️𖥔 ݁✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆

Present day

The next few days were a nightmare playing on loop and Phainon didn't have a remote to pause it. He stayed locked up in his room, sleeping fitfully most of the time and devouring snacks nearing their expiration date when he was awake. The rage he felt at himself for being so disgusting never left.

It looked back at him when he looked into the mirror. It terrorised him when he was asleep.

But he was fine. He was always fine— and never anything but. Even as his life burned down, he sat and watched because he didn't deserve anything else.

He ignored the calls that began to pile up and eventually, blocked everyone's contacts. Phainon didn't have the heart to block Mydei's email, so he did see the notifications, but never read them. Sometimes, he scrolled through social media through an anonymous account and read through the online discussions about him. He deliberately avoided the excessively aggressive ones— his self hatred was more than enough, thank you very much.

"Black Tide creature in disguise"

As if.

"We have been played as fools by this charming charlatan"

Charming? Him?

"DieDieDieDieDieDieDie Phainon you monster"

…

That one slipped through the cracks. Next.

"I heard he lived in Styxia, you know, with all the monsters around him. Maybe that's where he got his liking for murder."

How did they even figure out about his past? He thought he hid it pretty well. But when you're Okhema's most hated person, people are bound to dig up dirt on you.

"CHRYSOS is probably gonna shut down because of him. I mean, everyone's lost faith in them bc of how badly he screwed up. I mean, killing three people? That's wild."

Yep, that's enough depressing posts for one day.

Phainon fell back onto the bed, sprawling out on the sheets. The sharp, stabbing pain of his blunder had turned into a dull ache. His eyes were rimmed with red permanently now and his eyes stung when he cried.

Checking his phone again, he saw yet another email from Mydei. Maybe it was morbid curiosity or pure loneliness, he read through the emails Mydei sent.

Mydei ˂mydei.389@email.com˃5:55 PM to me▼

Phainon, where did you go? Please, I just want to talk.

Mydei ˂mydei.389@email.com˃5:57 PM to me▼

I heard you're in your dorm room, is that true?

Mydei ˂mydei.389@email.com˃6:15 PM to me▼

I know you don't want to talk to anyone right now, but trust me when I say, none of this is your fault.

Mydei ˂mydei.389@email.com˃7:01 AM to me▼

It kept him alive in Styxia. It kept him fighting for Okhema. Everyone he loved was preserved perfectly in glass within his memories and his memories alone— at least, that what he thought.

All he had now was the idea of them.

And all they were now was a festering wound that he had learned to live with.

It was Mydei's words that brought him out of his spiral. "I don't remember what my mother looked like or sounded like either. All I recall are the memories of her and the things she told me. People remain stuck in the past once they die and it's only their fading memory that you can carry forward. That's thing about loss— loss isn't just the person, it's your memories of them too."

"To me, losing their memories feels like moving on." Phainon's voice was strained as he said his next words." I don't want to move on from them. I can't move on from them; not after how they were taken from me and how bad things got once they were gone."

He instantly regretting spilling his guts out to Mydei. It felt so wrong to have someone else be privy to your innermost thoughts.

"You don't have to move on. You could try to accept that they're gone and you're alive right now. You're not in the wrong for wanting a good future for yourself."

Phainon didn't know that was an option. He swallowed the lump in his throat.

"So what now?" He asked, "CHRYSOS will never have to function as a facility and the people have no need for a disgraced saviour."

"You could live your own life. Do whatever you want to do. I'm sure you once had dreams beyond sacrificing every part of yourself to the public."

Phainon couldn't remember what he had wanted for himself.

"Your mother" Phainon said, trying to change the topic."What did she tell you, Mydei?"

Mydei looked up at the stars. "To not let rage be the only thing that drives me forward."

"She.. sounds like a knowledgeable woman."

Mydei wore a soft, nostalgic smile— a rare sight. "Indeed. she was the most remarkable person I have ever known."

From the way Mydei spoke of her, he clearly loved her. Whoever his mother was, she would be so proud of the boy she raised. Phainon was sure of it.

"Castorice and Hyacine want to talk to you, Phainon."

"And if they hate me now? "

"They don't. Talk to them. They care for you— they even made that collection of supportive comments for you. If that doesn't mean that you are valued, then I don't know what does."

"Okay, okay. I can do this. I can do—"

"—don't tell me you have cold feet now, HKS."

Phainon scoffed, lying through his teeth. "Absolutely not. I'm going now and I will resolve this. You'll see, Mydei." He stalked off.

Phainon walked through the pitch black hall of of unconscious guards— his phones' flashlight being the only thing he could use to brave his way through. He had asked the Kremnoan reinforcements Mydei called called in about the whereabouts of either a purple haired girl or a pink haired medic. They said the pink haired medic was with a quote "unhinged teal guy with an eye patch" on the fifth floor.

Good enough.

He shone the flashlight at a flurry of movement to his left and shrieked when it landed on someone's face. Professor Anaxa was decidedly very unimpressed at having a bright light shone into his eye.

"Hyacine's finishing up gathering the documents down the hall." Anaxa grumbled "Go and get that light out of my eye unless you want to blind me."

"Sorry, Prof A." Phainon said his apologies and hightailed it out of there before Anaxa decided to turn him into his next research subject out of spite.

"Hyacine?" Phainon said to the darkness. Damn the power in this building. They could've waited a bit longer to shut off the power.

He let out another high pitched shriek when someone tapped his shoulder, nearly dropping his phone.

"Sorry, I thought you were Professor Anaxa here to chew me out—" He explained sheepishly before all words failed him as he came face to face with Hyacine. All the excuses he had concocted seemed wrong.

"We need to talk. Now." said Hyacine

Phainon nodded mutely. It occurred to him that the blood was still on him. As if he needed yet another reason for Hyacine to hate him.

"Did you find him?" Castorice walked out of a door, carrying a torch. Her expression steeled when she saw Phainon. She looked to Hyacine, who nodded.

Hyacine too a deep breath."Phainon. You keep everyone at arm's length. You're there for us whenever we text you, but we know nothing and I mean nothing about you. When you got into that fight and had to move out of your dorm room, did you tell us a thing? Did you tell us when you were struggling or when you were grieving or sad? Did you let us help? "

Phainon hung his head. "I'm sorry. You guys mean a lot to me and I just didn't want to burden you with my problems. "

"You are not a burden. You need to learn how to trust other people."

As if anything's ever that simple. He can't just go and undo the distrustfulness that kept him alive and sane all these years. It would be like ripping away a part of himself.

"Or at least, try to believe that we care about you. Can you do that much?"

"First, ouch, I'm not a child. And second— fine. I will." Phainon knew he looked pathetic, asking them this, "Do you hate me now?"

Castorice shook her head. "Hate you? Phainon, we don't hate you and never will. Just tell us if something's wrong. Nothing you say would make us see you any differently."

"So is this you guys forgiving me?" Phainon asked.

"Yes." Hyacine confirmed.

Phainon sighed in relief and held his arms open. Castorice and Hyacine hugged him without protest.

"Thank you for dealing with me for all these years "

"Don't mention it." Castorice smiled. "Glad to have you back."

Normalcy was something Phainon had never known, but this was the closest he felt to it.

Chapter End Notes

We're finally down to one more chapter!!! Writing this has been a journey, I'll tell you that. I started this months ago(like in July) and it's only now that I'm nearly done with it.

Once Phainon fell into silence, he continued, "We've sent out agents to neutralise the remaining Black Tide creatures, so the regions outside Okhema are no longer dangerous. Aglaea is sponsoring a trip for you. You are free to go wherever you please."

He was going to see Mydei again— which was stupid, because he had hung out with Mydei the night before.

"Mydei!" Phainon couldn't run towards Mydei fast enough. "Pack your bags, we're going to Aedes Elysiae!"

"Huh?"

"I got paid vacation time!"

"So you think that I'm not busy? Go bother Castorice or Hyacine."

Phainon rolled his eyes. "Oh come on, you're not that busy. Plus, Cas and Cinny are really busy. Please?"

"No."

"Please?"

"No."

"How many more times must I say please before you agree?"

"Go on, then. Try convincing me."

Phainon took a deep breath "Pleasepleasepleaseplease—"

"—pleasepleaseplease—" His voice grew louder.

Mydei winced, clenching his fist.

"—pleasepleaseplease—"

People around them craned their heads, trying to get a better look at the scene.

Upon noticing the scrutiny they were under, Mydei held a hand up, signaling him to stop; probably trying to stop the embarrassment. "When are we leaving?"

Phainon grinned.

"When you said we were going to Aedes Elysiae, I didn't think it would be on the same day"

Phainon paid no heed to him, instead admiring the view as the train rattled past countrysides. Greens blurred with the soft pastel blue of the sky, the multicoloured settlements whizzing by. Life was strange in its resilience, towns holding up through the advent and the retreat of the Black Tide. Phainon was tense; Mydei could sense it in his gait and cloudy eyes. He steadied the obnoxiously large backpack he'd packed; it threatened to topple over with every lurch of the train.

Phainon leaped up as soon as the train screeched to a halt. "This is an outpost near Aedes Elysiae. We'll have to travel on foot from here."

Mydei had to strain his ears to hear what Phainon was saying over the chaos of the train.

The air felt different here. Crisp.

Black marks eroded patches of soil, but there was a peace Mydei had yet to see anywhere else. Life in Okhema ran by too fast and the places his detachment visited were either abandoned or infested with creatures. Life felt strange now that yet another one of his goals was gone. First it was to kill his father, then it as to settle his people into Okhema. Now, the Black Tide too.

Phainon got off the train first, starting the walk. Mydei walked behind him, taking in the scenery. Fields stretched endlessly into the horizon. The sun was high up in. Mydei himself had no idea where they were headed to, but Phainon seemed to know, effortlessly navigating through the wheat fields.

"I brought a tent so we could have a place to sleep if the village has fallen into disrepair. Plus some supplies if there aren't any places nearby for us to get food." Phainon explained, holding out a hand to skim the wheat that rose to their knees.

"I brought supplies too. No tents, though." Mydei said. The poles of his tent made a slight tinkling sound as they clinked against each other in his backpack.

Phainon inspected the wheat. "Someone cultivates these."

Mydei looked around, trying to find some form of settlement beyond the fields bathed in gold.

Phainon was bathed in a golden halo too. His white hair looked iridescent as it swayed with the breeze and caught the sunlight. His eyes a shade of sapphire blue that even the sky would be jealous of. In the midst of the endless acres of gold, Phainon fit right in. Like he was born to be made of light . Phaenon, the brightest star in the sky.

Phaenon, of endless light.

"Mydei!" Phainon jabbed Mydei's side.

"Son of a— what was that for?"Mydei frowned heavily.

"You didn't listen to me the first few times I called your name."

"So you thought that jabbing my side was the best way to catch my attention?"

"I just wanted to see your reaction." Phainon said blithely

"Hmph. Foolhardy pest."

"Speaking of pests, there are a bunch of aphids and armyworms around here. Hope you don't hate bugs."

"The only bug I hate is you."

"You wound me, my darling Mydei. And here I thought you loved me"

That Mydei did.

"Found it!" Phainon exclaimed. Realisation washed over his face as he squinted to get a better look. "Let's uh, go somewhere else."

"Why?"

"No reason." Phainon croaked.

"Are you trying to avoid that house? Or perhaps the person who lives in that house?"

Phainon's expression was pained, a cross between reluctance and frustration. "Damn you." He muttered.

"But seriously though, why do you care so much about this particular house?"

"I don't. I don't care." Phainon protested.

"Oh yeah? Then why do I have to physically haul you there?" Mydei tugged on the strap of Phainon's backpack to continue their slow procession to the small house.

"Look me dead in the eye and try to figure out how many fucks I give about this place." Without giving Mydei a chance to respond, Phainon replied, "Zero. That's right. Zero."

It was when Mydei's hand hovered over the doorbell that Phainon cracked.

"No, Mydei. Please, reconsider. We can uh— go there! Look! Wheat! I wanna go there—"

"HKS, what is up with you?"

Phainon would have made a run for it when the door of the house creaked open if it wasn't for Mydei's firm grip on his backpack.

A middle aged lady stood at the door, squinting to see the visitors. Her eyes widened in shock upon noticing Phainon. Her circular glasses dropped from the bridge of her nose as she stared at Phainon like she was seeing a ghost.

"Child, is that you?"

"I—" Phainon looked helplessly at Mydei, pleading him to save him. "Yes."

"You're alive." The woman's owlish face broke into a warm smile. "I always knew you would be."

"Why don't you two come in?"

"Oh, no—We wouldn't want to intrude—"

"Nonsense. There's hardly anyone nearby. I'm elated to have guests."

Her house was small. A single dining table sat in the center, with seats for two. Pictures and memorabilia lined the walls. A small room with a bed was connected to the main hall. The house smelled like sandalwood and incense.

Phainon trailed after her, offering to help her serve tea and snacks. When Mydei offered to do the same, he was met with fierce resistance so he sat on a pile of baskets at the dining table. Phainon eventually joined him— Mydei suspected that he was turned away from the kitchen too.

Phainon shifted guiltily, his long limbs jutting out of place in the small seat. He looked like he would rather be anywhere than here. He threw nervous glances at the old lady, like he was waiting for all hell to break loose again.

"But I thought they closed all rail lines from Okhema?" She asked, emerging from the kitchen with a cracked porcelain tray.

"They reopened them last night. Everyone's trying to visit their old homes or graves of their loved ones." Mydei explained.

The old woman placed a cup of tea in front of Mydei."So Okhema's finally open to the outside world, huh?"

"Yes. The creatures are gone.""

The woman sighed , like a heavy burden was finally off her shoulders.

"You're not going to ask any more questions?"

"And what good will the answers to those questions be to me? You, on the other hand, look like you have a plethora of them."

"Say, how did you survive out here?" Mydei asked ,"From Styxia to parts of Kremnos, The Black Tide creatures were everywhere."

"They receded in the outskirts of Okhema a long time ago. Probably thought they killed every person out there." She chuckled wryly. "A few of us were at the farmers' market a few towns over when the creatures struck Aedes Elysiae. We were told that we couldn't return since Aedes Elysiae had fallen. I couldn't accept my family's death, so I made the journey back. "

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be. Someone had dug graves for the deceased— it's off in the outcropping. At the very least, they were honoured in their deaths."

Phainon looked as though he might shatter like fine china.

The words came tumbling out, like Phainon was reliving them all over again.

I'm sorry I couldn't save your daughter." Phainon hung his head. Mydei knew he would never understand how deep the regret must have embedded itself into Phainon. He would never understand most of what made Phainon — the persistence, the sense of justice, the unhinged rage.

"You were a child. Be kinder to yourself, Phainon." She said gently.

"But, even then—"

"No. You have nothing to be sorry about."

Mydei watched Phainon's fingers whiten as they curled into fists.

"Be honest. Years ago, would you have blamed me for not saving your daughter had you found out I got out as the only one unscathed?"

Without missing a beat, she nodded. "Yes. I would have. I would have wondered why she didn't survive in your place."

Somehow, Phainon seemed to find comfort in that. Words that should have stung like daggers were what he willingly embraced. He smiled, light and free. Was he… comfortable around scathing words? No, not comfortable, but used to it. Like this was where he was supposed to be and nothing more.

"But time is a funny thing, isn't it?" She said. "Now, I can't imagine why I could hate the sweetest kid I've ever known. I hope my words didn't offend you."

Phainon waved his hand dismissively. "No offense taken!"

Mydei may never understand Phainon, but he would forever think of him as the strongest person he's ever met. After all, it takes a strong person to be so gentle after all this pain.

Phainon sprung up, muttering something vague.

"It feels like just yesterday when he was a little boy who couldn't wait to save the world because of a prophecy his older sister gave him. A little prediction. Most people would have thought of it as a momentary fascination, but this one thought differently. He'd go out of his way to help us with mundane jobs, keep the younger ones entertained and run around playing hero. Those actions— they weren't childish, they were honest. He wanted to save the world." The woman said, once Phainon had disappeared out of sight.

"That he did. He was— and still is— a hero to Okhema."

Her face softened into a small smile. "So he did it after all."

"Yes." Mydei found himself missing Phainon's presence next to him.

"He's a good man, Mydei. Treat him well."

Mydei choked on air.

"We aren't— like that"

"It didn't look that way to me."

When Phainon returned, his eyes looked more red rimmed than usual. His annoyingly perfect smile was perfectly intact.

The house reverberated with Phainon's excited chatter— something about Okhema and reminiscing the past— Mydei was too busy admiring Phainon to pay proper attention. The sun was back, bright and cheerful as ever. Unbothered and glorious, he laughed. Like nothing had ever hurt him before.

He will never mention that he found Phainon holding Dawnmaker to his forehead the night after he killed Caenis, begging for mercy or for salvation, he would never know.

Nostalgia was a bittersweet thing, it creeped up into your heart and tugged at it like a vine. Nostalgia was the rustling of the wheat fields, the chirping of the cicadas in the summer, the lemon drops a kind old lady gave the kids as they traipsed into her house to rest after playing.

Relief was a tide.

It would never wash away the jagged lines of hurt, but it would at least make them feel less painful.

Auntie Adara, that was her name, managed the sprawling wheat fields. She had the same brown eyes that crinkled at the corners and the blunt honesty Phainon remembered. He had offered to help her with her wheat fields, even if it was for a week or two. She called him dutiful and kind; he called himself selfish for wanting to relive his past.

Mydei and Phainon set up camp outside her small house. Phainon's tent should have been enough accommodate two normal people, but things got a bit dicey with two tall men who'd been trained to fight their entire lives.

The next morning was a much needed reprieve from the excruciating

"Come on!" Phainon yelled to Mydei, who loitered around the outskirts of the wheat fields. Phainon held a scythe in one hand, another hand holding down his straw hat, keeping it from flying away with the billowing winds.

"Yes, yes, on my way." Mydei trudged to Phainon, stalking through the wheat.

"Auntie Adara told us to harvest that patch of land first." Phainon leaned toward Mydei, pointing it out. Mydei stiffened, but didn't pull away. "Think you can handle that, princey?"

"Never call me that."

"I've called you darling on emails. I'm sure you can handle the nickname princey."

Mydei sputtered "Don't say that out loud—"

"Oh? Why not?" Phainon chuckled, clearing his throat before yelling to no one at all— "I CALL MYDEI DARLING! HA!"

Mydei's fists curled up into balls, like he was ready to throw hands right then and there.

"No one heard. Shame." Phainon sighed.

"Shame? As if you have any of that."

"Ouch, Mydei. Low blow." He shook his head dramatically.

"Just— just do something." Mydei sniffed.

"You mean harvest?"

"Yes. That."

"Your wish is my command, princey."

"Knock it off or I knock off your head."

"Realistically, though" said Phainon as he gathered a bundle of wheat in his arms" Can you punch someone's head off?"

"Why are we talking about this right now?"

"Shush. Answer the question."

"Want me to test it out on you?" Mydei heaved a bundle of wheat onto his shoulder. That had no right being that hot. And distracting.

Scratch that, it was Mydei's very existence that was distracting.

They headed to the granary.

"Want to go to the nearby town?" Phainon asked, dusting his overalls, "Auntie told me that there's a small town nearby with a bar and a market."

"All right. But you're paying"

"Cheapskate, but it was my offer. So fine, I'll be gracious and pay for you."

"My hero" Mydei scoffed. The world 'hero' should have felt like poison after all this, but he found himself surprisingly okay.

From the open window, Phainon could see that outcropping. The one that felt like a hot iron brand on his skin. He was too much of a coward to go there so he followed Mydei back out of the granary.

✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ 𖥔 ݁☀️𖥔 ݁✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ Years ago

Small hands trembled as they scrambled to dig up the earth. Mud caked under them, coagulating with the blood. His blood or their blood, he didn't know anymore. The actions were automatic, like he'd spent a lifetime digging graves and burying the deceased. Like he wasn't a child who had spent all his short years alive adored by the people he now had to send off. Ten down, five to go. Each adult body was too big for a child to drag and yet he managed to carry them anyways.

It was burying Cyrene that broke him.

Her sweet smile lost to the past, pink hair dyed red at the ends. Eyes open, glassy and unknowing, her skin of a pallor and stiff like he'd only seen on dead animals in the fields. And yet, her voice and the life she once had was a recent memory he would claw at to keep afloat.

He hoped she would know what he would do to bring her back and how much he missed her. But dead people are dead and forever unaware of the living. They will never know who grieved them or laid by their graves for hours, trying to wring every last bit of warmth out of their presence before the air got too cold and so did their hearts and they had to leave.

This wasn't supposed to happen.

They were supposed to grow up and do everything together. They were supposed to celebrate more birthdays together, play make believe in the fields where Phainon was the hero and Cyrene was his trusted guide and—-

She was supposed to be alive. She was supposed to be right next to him— a permanent fixture in his life. Not six feet under. They should've grown up together.

Even if their jobs turn out to be soul crushing and lack the luster of childhood, they would still have each other. Life is made beautiful by the people in it, so everything he saw right then was horribly revolting to him.

That was where he stayed for a long time: hunched over, hands clasped, shoulders shaking, begging whatever Titan would listen for it to please be him too.

Nobody answered.

Had he been a believer of divinity, he would have lost all faith.

Yet here he stood, the unholy spawn that they forgot to kill.

✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ 𖥔 ݁☀️𖥔 ݁✶⋆.˚⋆⭒˚.⋆ Present day

The sun dipped below the horizon as he and Mydei reached the town. Nobody knew who they were and nobody cared. Life was slow; the locals strolling leisurely as they went about their day. Children ran back home from the park for dinner.

At the bar, Mydei took a sip of the drink and his upper lip curled in disgust as he set the glass down.

"Ugh. This stings. How are you able to choke that down?"

"Oh, this? Quite easily, actually. My sense of taste, uh, let's just say that scavenging and eating scraps in Styxia did a number on it."

Realisation passed through Mydei's features.

"So… you couldn't taste anything I made for you?"

"Not exactly, but hey! I can still taste pretty good food, so it's still a win. Wait, no— are you mad at me for not being able to taste your food? I'm sorry, trust me, I loved it!"

"No, you fucking idiot. I don't cook for just anyone. I cook for you because I know you like my food. I just didn't know you couldn't taste it. "

Phainon couldn't stand looking at Mydei anymore, afraid of what he would see. "Well, now you know!"

He then busied himself with swirling the drink and watching the ice melt.

Mydei went silent for a long time. Silence was the norm with Mydei, but this silence was more pensive. Contemplative. He downed one glass of vodka. And then another. Truly, his resistance to alcohol was one to be reckoned with.

"I will never get to know everything about you, will I?" Mydei said, resigned. He placed yet another glass down on the counter.

"Is that… really that important to you? Knowing everything about me?" Phainon said slowly.

"It may not seem like much to you, but yes. I want to know all there is to know about you. That is the way I show that I care."

"Blunt as always, huh, Mydei?" Phainon hid the blush on his cheeks by looking down at the drink and letting his hair hide his face. "Whatever happened to you hating my guts?"

"I still think you're an asshole. But you're a mildly tolerable, self sacrificing one."

"That almost sounds like praise."

"If I knew how to praise you properly, I would."

The number of times Mydei had made Phainon's heart soar with hope that should never have been there needed to be studied. This meant nothing. This had to mean nothing. Mydei was tipsy and so was Phainon. Just a bout of drunk honesty, nothing more.

Phainon stumbled, giggling giddily as Mydei hauled him out. One of Mydei's hands were hooked under Phainon's arm to stabilise him.

"Be grateful I'm lugging your ass out of here."

"Ah, but you love me too much to leave me stranded in the drains." Phainon drawled, staring up at the sky. It looked a lot prettier without all the pollution fogging up the stars.

"Trust me, I absolutely would do that. A very tempting choice, if you ask me." Mydei kicked Phainon's shin as he stumbled "HKS! Don't trip on flat land!"

"Ow" Phainon whined, leaning his head on Mydei's shoulder. "Comfort me for the emotional and physical damage you have inflicted upon me."

"What? You gonna sue me for that?" Mydei was suddenly trying very hard to not look at Phainon
